economic.label: Economic history
economic.date_label: 1800s roots · Economic History Society founded 1926 · multiple paradigms
economic.description: Competing explanations investigate institutions, prices and incomes, class relations, growth, households, slavery and empire. Serial history and cliometrics use different questions and models. North’s incentives differ from Polanyi’s historically specific market society; Gerschenkron questions repeated industrial paths; de Vries connects household labor and demand; Pomeranz combines regional comparison with global resource relations.
economic.representative_figures_and_works: Nineteenth-century roots include classical political economy and the German historical school (e.g. Schmoller); twentieth-century examples include R. H. Tawney, Eileen Power, and Douglass North. Further approaches include Polanyi, The Great Transformation (1944); Gerschenkron, Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection); de Vries’s industrious-revolution article (1994); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000). E. A. Wrigley: People, Cities and Wealth (1987); Continuity, Chance and Change (1988).

strands.works: Schmoller’s methodological review (1883); Cunningham’s textbook (1882); Ashley and disciplinary institutions

strands.title: British economic and social history
strands.focus: Economic life studied through social relations, belief, households, and women’s work.
strands.works: Tawney, Religion and the Rise of Capitalism; Power, Medieval People; Clark and Pinchbeck on women’s labour

strands.title: French serial and conjunctural history
strands.focus: Simiand and Labrousse investigate different economic movements. Later rereadings distinguish construction of evidence, causal conditions and routine series; uneven crises need not fit one automatic sequence.
strands.works: Esquisse du mouvement des prix et des revenus en France au XVIIIe siècle (1933); La crise de l’économie française à la fin de l’Ancien Régime et au début de la Révolution (1944); “Panoramas de la crise” (1956); Grenier/Lepetit (1989); Simonin (1992)

strands.title: Capitalist development and contested production relations
strands.focus: Coercion, markets, wage labour and the state are related explanatory problems. Dobb’s reply acknowledges uncertainty about one accumulation hypothesis; Sweezy and Takahashi pose different challenges.
strands.works: Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); reply to Sweezy in “The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism” (1950), pp. 157–167; Takahashi (1952); Unwin (1904)

strands.title: Cliometrics and historical measurement
strands.focus: Economic models and quantitative evidence; neither all economic history nor all quantitative history.
strands.works: Fogel, “Economic Growth, Population Theory, and Physiology” (1993); North, “Economic Performance through Time” (1993)

strands.title: Institutions and economic change
strands.focus: Rules, incentives, learning, and historical paths; overlaps with cliometrics without being identical to it.
strands.works: North, Economic Performance through Time

strands.title: Slavery, empire, and unequal development
strands.focus: Different arguments about capitalist development and colonial power; Drescher contests the decline explanation for British slave-trade abolition.
strands.works: Capitalism and Slavery (1944); How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972); Econocide (1977)

strands.title: Market society and nonmarket economic relations
strands.focus: Polanyi distinguishes a market-regulated economy from reciprocity and redistribution; his broad historical claims are arguments to examine, not settled descriptions of every society.
strands.works: The Great Transformation (1944), chapter IV

strands.title: Different paths of later industrialization
strands.focus: Compare technology borrowing, industrial scale and the roles of banks and states; later industrializers need not repeat England’s sequence.
strands.works: Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection)

strands.title: Household labor, demand and industrious change
strands.focus: Changes in household resource allocation can increase market labor and demand together. Household members’ interests differ, and the proposed pattern is not universal.
strands.works: “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution” (1994)

strands.title: Regional comparison and global divergence
strands.focus: Pomeranz compares developed regions within Eurasia and connects divergence with coal and overseas resources, avoiding an undifferentiated Europe-versus-Asia contrast.
strands.works: The Great Divergence (2000)

strands.title: Material life, markets and capitalism
strands.focus: Braudel distinguishes overlapping economic activities and geographically centered world-economies. His disagreement with Weber and selective Wallerstein dialogue are attributed arguments, not a settled universal history.
strands.works: Afterthoughts on Material Civilization and Capitalism (1977)

strands.title: Market norms and popular action
strands.focus: Thompson asks how customary expectations authorize or constrain protest and exchange; Mintz supplies a named anthropological resource. This is a situated inquiry into English crowds, not a universal premarket economy.
strands.works: “The Moral Economy of the English Crowd” (1971)

strands.title: Agrarian change and documentary comparability
strands.focus: Tawney distinguishes regional and temporal patterns, tenant and landlord activity, legal forms and economic pressures. His introduction treats incomplete statistics and incompatible records as problems of inference.
strands.works: The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912), introduction

strands.title: Women’s work, household forms and economic change
strands.focus: Clark and Pinchbeck distinguish home production from wages, while differing over the timing and consequences of economic change. Their acknowledgments make research guidance and shared materials part of this scholarship.
strands.works: Working Life of Women (1919); Women Workers (1930)

strands.title: Domestic service as an economic question
strands.focus: Salmon connects household employment with industrial specialization and challenges its reduction to a private complaint. Her historical model and proposed remedies are arguments to assess, not a universal account of women’s experience.
strands.works: Domestic Service (1897), chapters I–II; Progress in the Household (1906), Apologia

strands.title: Brazilian income flows and structural criticism
strands.focus: Furtado’s coffee-crisis argument connects demand and historical change; Novais asks how wage labour and capitalism’s formation explain the transformation. Their exchange keeps macroeconomic analysis open to historical criticism.
strands.works: Furtado (1959/2005), XXXI–XXXII opening; Novais (1961)

strands.title: Managerial coordination and the scale of activity
strands.focus: Chandler’s selected opening links new energy, transport and communication capacities to the conditions for administrative coordination. Earlier growth and specialization could remain compatible with owner-managed firms and market exchange.
strands.works: The Visible Hand (1977), Part I and chapter1 opening

strands.title: Artisans and uneven industrialization in India
strands.focus: Roy examines five crafts rather than treating textile decline as universal. His introduction distinguishes family work, wage labour, markets and organizational change, while acknowledging that adaptation did not yield development comparable to Europe or Japan.
strands.works: Traditional Industry in the Economy of Colonial India (1999), introduction

strands.title: Firms, inventions and forms of work
strands.focus: Compare Chandler’s American enterprise scale, Mokyr’s British technological change and Roy’s Indian artisanal reorganization. These explanations concern different units and periods; none supplies a universal sequence from household to large factory.
strands.works: Chandler (1977); Mokyr (1999); Roy (1999), selected primary passages

strands.title: Railroads and the meaning of social saving
strands.focus: McClelland contests identifying measured transport savings with the railroad’s entire contribution to growth. His notes question the relation between observed freight prices and marginal costs under altered traffic and competition.
strands.works: Railroads and American Economic Growth (1964); McClelland (1968), opening and notes

strands.title: Slavery productivity and a contested inference
strands.focus: Fogel and Engerman’s opening specifies a total-factor-productivity index. David and Temin argue that national-price aggregation across differing crop mixes need not rank technical efficiency: climate, prices and risk complicate the inference.
strands.works: Fogel/Engerman (1977), opening; David/Temin (1979),213–214

strands.title: Household production and disputed divergence
strands.focus: Pomeranz challenges Huang’s involution thesis and compares household labor with industrious change. Huang’s 2002 review argues that output growth can conceal diminishing returns to work; Pomeranz’s reply opening rejects one necessary path to development.
strands.works: Pomeranz (2000),17; Huang and Pomeranz (2002), selected retrospective passages; Huang’s rejoinder and Pomeranz’s response (2003)

strands.title: Coal, constraints and competing explanations
strands.focus: Pomeranz links accessible energy and colonial resources to relief of land constraints. Huang questions whether coal availability explains divergence or industrial demand explains coal development. The exchange leaves causal weights open to examination.

strands.title: Wealth and the measurement of goods
strands.focus: Weatherill acknowledges Shammas’s challenge: ownership patterns associated with occupation or towns may reflect wealth. Their different data constructions ask different questions.
strands.works: Weatherill (1996),xviii–xix and notes17,20

strands.title: Agrarian labour and recorded categories
strands.focus: Kumar’s southern Indian inquiry combines documentary interpretation with quantitative reconstruction. Her stated caste/occupation assumptions must remain visible when discussing estimates.
strands.works: Land and Caste in South India (1965), opening extracts I,IV,X

strands.title: Population and the character of industrial growth
strands.focus: Wrigley investigates population change and the contingent character of industrial growth. This bounded summary follows the Economic History Society account and the publisher excerpts of Continuity, Chance and Change (1988, pp. 1–8) and Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010, pp. 1–6, 9–11); People, Cities and Wealth (1987) is unread.
strands.works: People, Cities and Wealth (1987); Continuity, Chance and Change (1988)

economic.scope_note: Distinguish the relevant historians, evidence, and mechanisms before claiming an influence. A subject shared with Annales or Marxism is not itself an explanation. Institutional approaches are not interchangeable, and consumption does not replace production. Household interests can conflict. Gerschenkron’s European comparison and Pomeranz’s Eurasian argument have distinct scales; neither is a universal development law. Furtado’s demand analysis and Novais’s structural criticism offer a Brazilian exchange, with primary-edition and numerical verification limits retained.

richard_white.label: Richard White
richard_white.date_label: Land Use, Environment, and Social Change 1980 · The Roots of Dependency 1983 · field survey 1985 · The Middle Ground 1991 · The Organic Machine 1995 · Remembering Ahanagran 1998 · spatial-history working paper 2010 · Railroaded 2011 · The Republic for Which It Stands 2017 · California Exposures book discussion 2020 · Who Killed Jane Stanford? 2022
richard_white.description: A historian of the American West, of Native American history and of environmental history. The Middle Ground (1991; quoted from Cambridge Core first-page excerpts of the introduction and chapters) rejects accounts of Indian–white contact with 'but two outcomes', conquest or persistence, because contact 'creates as well as destroys': in the Great Lakes pays d'en haut, French and Algonquian allies 'had to arrive at some common conception of suitable ways of acting', a middle ground which White describes as a process of creative and often expedient misunderstanding, sustained because whites could not simply command Indians or disregard them, until in the nineteenth century its compromises 'yielded to stark choices between assimilation and otherness'. His environmental books trace Salish and settler land use and environmental change in Island County, Washington (1980), subsistence, environment and dependency among the Choctaws, Pawnees and Navajos (1983), and the Columbia River as an organic machine, an energy system remade by human labour that keeps natural qualities, in which human work is energy as much as the river's flow (1995). His 1985 Pacific Historical Review essay surveyed environmental history as a new field, and he responded to Worster's agroecological essay in the 1990 Journal of American History round table. His later work also addresses memory, capitalism and American national history. Remembering Ahanagran (1998; 2003 paperback) examines family recollection against historical evidence, according to its publisher’s account. The companion description of Railroaded (2011) connects railway corporations, debt, political patronage, economic instability and western landscapes; the book itself is not read here. His 2010 working paper treats collaborative digital visualization as a method of historical research. The later selection includes The Republic for Which It Stands (2017), California Exposures (documented in 2020, with photographs by Jesse Amble White) and Who Killed Jane Stanford? (2022).
richard_white.representative_figures_and_works: Richard White (b. 1947); Land Use, Environment, and Social Change: The Shaping of Island County, Washington (1980; 1992 paperback with Cronon's foreword and a new preface); The Roots of Dependency: Subsistence, Environment, and Social Change among the Choctaws, Pawnees, and Navajos (1983); “American Environmental History: The Development of a New Historical Field” (1985); “Environmental History, Ecology, and Meaning” (1990); The Middle Ground: Indians, Empires, and Republics in the Great Lakes Region, 1650–1815 (1991); The Organic Machine: The Remaking of the Columbia River (1995); “‘Are You an Environmentalist or Do You Work for a Living?’” (1995). Readings: Savard (1992), Edmunds (1993) and D. R. Miller (1994) on The Middle Ground; Cronon's foreword (1992) to Land Use. Later and additional selected works: “It’s Your Misfortune and None of My Own”: A New History of the American West (1991); Remembering Ahanagran: Storytelling in a Family’s Past (1998; Washington paperback as A History of Stories, 2003, foreword by William Cronon); “The Nationalization of Nature” (1999); “What is Spatial History?” (2010 working paper); Railroaded: The Transcontinentals and the Making of Modern America (2011); The Republic for Which It Stands (2017); California Exposures: Envisioning Myth and History (documented in 2020, photographs by Jesse Amble White); Who Killed Jane Stanford? (2022).
richard_white.scope_note: Not Hayden White (node white). Witnesses for The Middle Ground: Cambridge Core first-page excerpts (full pages, folios observed) of the introduction (1991 p. ix) and of the chapters opening at pp. 50, 94 and 518; the next page of the introduction (1991 p. x = 2011 p. xxvi) and pp. 52–53 and 93 only in Google Books search-within snippets of the 2011 twentieth-anniversary edition, whose body pagination matches 1991 at the pages checked (the equation 1991 p. x = 2011 p. xxvi is inferred from the introduction's opening at 1991 p. ix and 2011 p. xxv). The rest of the book is unread, and wording witnessed only by snippets is paraphrased in node text. Land Use (1980; 1992 paperback) and The Organic Machine (1995) are known from Google Books search-within snippets of their framing pages, not from page images; The Organic Machine's preface folios were not visible, so its framing is paraphrased. The Roots of Dependency (1983), the 1985 survey, the 1990 round-table response and the 1995 Uncommon Ground essay are unread (paywalled or not previewed) and are known through Cronon (1993, 1994), Worster (1990, Portuguese translation), Cook (1990), Isenberg (2013) and the publisher's records. He is not presented as a founder of environmental history: Land Use credits James Malin's neglected Great Plains studies as a trail to follow (snippet, p. 7), and Isenberg (2013) names him in a group of synthesisers. The middle ground was contested in period: Savard (1992) doubts its premise of Iroquois devastation, Edmunds (1993) finds the post-1770 chapters 'less convincing', and D. R. Miller (1994) notes the neglect of peoples neither Iroquoian nor Algonquian; Merrell's in-period critique (Into the American Woods, 1999) is known here only through White's later 2011 response. capitalismdebates.description: A set of linked arguments about why capitalism, industrialisation and Western wealth arose where and when they did. Marxist historians disputed whether trade or class relations ended feudalism: Dobb answered Sweezy that trade worked 'to the extent that it accentuated the internal conflicts' (1950). Brenner's property-relations thesis (1976) opened a second round, in which Bois called his approach 'political Marxism' and Wood made it a programme. Economic historians slowed the British Industrial Revolution while reasserting 'an important discontinuity' (Crafts and Harley, 1992), and Berg and Hudson answered that growth accounting had 'mis-specified' it; explanations multiplied in Wrigley's escape from an 'organic economy', de Vries's 'industrious revolution', Mokyr's 'Industrial Enlightenment' and Allen's high wages and cheap energy. Wong challenged Europe's status as the comparative norm; Pomeranz acknowledged that method while giving greater weight to global conjunctures, ecological constraints, coal and New World resources; critics answered from property relations, knowledge, wages and the state. Williams's Capitalism and Slavery (1944) returned through Inikori, the Legacies of British Slave-ownership project and an American 'history of capitalism' whose economic-historian critics charged 'specious arguments' (Hilt, 2017). Readers join these debates themselves: Burnard and Riello set the new history of capitalism beside the Brenner debate and Pomeranz (2020).

strands.title: The transition debate: Dobb, Sweezy and their readers, 1946–1976
strands.focus: Dobb's Studies (1946) defined feudalism by the coercive relation between producer and lord; Sweezy (1950) answered that feudalism was 'a system of production for use' dissolved by 'causes external to the system', above all trade, while granting that 'no theory which fails to take into account the factors which Dobb stresses … can be regarded as correct'. Dobb replied that trade 'exercised its influence to the extent that it accentuated the internal conflicts', and carried the argument to the absolutist state and the English Revolution. Takahashi (1952) developed an analysis of production relations and the social form of labour, and pressed for fuller French and German comparison. Hilton collected the exchange with later essays in 1976. Positions within one Marxist debate, not a school. The field strands marx/transition and economic/marxist keep each author's own contribution.
strands.works: Dobb, Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); Sweezy and Dobb, Science & Society 14:2 (1950): 134–167; Takahashi (1952); Merrington, 'Town and Country in the Transition to Capitalism' (NLR, 1975); Hilton (ed.), The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism (1976); see marx/transition and economic/marxist

strands.title: Against 'neo-Smithian Marxism': Brenner on Sweezy, Frank and Wallerstein, 1977
strands.focus: Brenner traced Wallerstein's world-system and Frank's development of underdevelopment back to Sweezy's side of the 1950 debate and, through it, to 'the model put forward by Adam Smith'. He acknowledged a 'great debt' to Dobb, and credited Frank with breaking 'the suffocating orthodoxies' of stage theory. Callinicos (1990) called the critique 'a valuable corrective'. See dependency/worldsystems for Wallerstein's own account.
strands.works: Brenner, NLR I/104 (1977); Wallerstein, The Modern World-System I (1974); Frank (1966–)

strands.title: The Brenner debate in Past and Present, 1976–1985
strands.focus: Brenner argued that class structure decides how demographic and commercial change affects growth. Postan and Hatcher called his charges against them 'groundless'; Le Roy Ladurie defended a 'neo-Malthusian' model; Croot and Parker, Wunder and Klíma tested his English, French, German and Bohemian comparisons; Bois agreed against 'the Malthusian model' but not with Brenner's method. Brenner's reply (1982) spoke of 'social-property systems'. Hilton introduced the collection (1985) as 'a continuation' of the transition debate. The respondents are read only in their Cambridge Core openings; their later pages are unread, and Bois's specified later passages (pp. 115–116) are known only as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos (1990); see annales/serial for Le Roy Ladurie's Languedoc.
strands.works: Past and Present 70 (1976) to 97 (1982); Aston and Philpin (eds), The Brenner Debate (1985)

strands.title: Political Marxism: from Bois's charge to a school, 1978–2016
strands.focus: Bois called Brenner's approach 'political Marxism', 'a voluntarist vision of history' (1978, as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos, 1990). By the accounts of Callinicos (1990) and Brenner (2016), Wood accepted the label while rejecting the charge of voluntarism. She argued that 'the economic' and 'the political' are differently joined in pre-capitalist and capitalist societies (1981), against G. A. Cohen's technological determinism. Critics answered that it was 'little more than a sociology of domination' (Callinicos) and that Brenner, taking up Dobb, narrowed class struggle to the countryside (Harman).
strands.works: Bois (1978); Wood, 'The Separation of the Economic and the Political in Capitalism' (NLR, 1981), Democracy Against Capitalism (1995); Harman (1989); Callinicos, 'The Limits of "Political Marxism"' (NLR, 1990); Harman and Brenner (2004, printed 2006); Brenner (2016) and Hirschkop (2016) on Wood

strands.title: The origin of capitalism and its critics, 1991–2004
strands.focus: Wood argued that England was 'the world's first capitalist society' (1991), siding with Thompson against the Nairn–Anderson theses. In 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001) she set the transition debate and Brenner's 'market dependence' against the 'commercialization model'; The Origin of Capitalism (1999; 2002), unread here, is known through its jacket and McAuley's quotations. McAuley (2001), drawing on Blaut, criticised 'the Brenner-Wood thesis' for treating colonialism as marginal; Wood replied that slave plantations mattered 'quite a while after the emergence of capitalism in the English countryside'. This exchange joins the strand to the slavery and divergence components.

strands.title: Revolution or gradual growth? The Industrial Revolution revised, 1884–1994
strands.focus: Toynbee's posthumous lectures (1884) defined the Industrial Revolution as 'the substitution of competition for the medieval regulations'. Crafts and Harley's output estimates slowed its pace while reasserting 'the industrial revolution as an important discontinuity' (1992); Berg and Hudson answered that growth accounting had 'mis-specified' the subject and left out women's and children's labour, regional specialisation and innovation (1990 working paper; 1992). De Vries (1994) read the revisionists as 'cleansing the temple of the "false god of the take off"', not pulling down the pillars.

strands.title: Rural industry and industrious households, 1972–2016
strands.focus: Mendels (1972) treated market-oriented rural industry as 'a first phase which preceded and prepared modern industrialization proper', and later called it 'a plausible and interesting set of hypotheses' (1984); the Göttingen group (Kriedte, Medick, Schlumbohm, 1977) placed rural industry in 'the genesis of capitalism'. Coleman (1983) titled his critique 'a concept too many'. De Vries's 'industrious revolution' (1994; 2008), a term he and van Nederveen Meerkerk trace to Akira Hayami, made household labour and demand precede the Industrial Revolution; reviewers asked whether consumption had become 'a new deus ex machina' (2009). Rosenband (2016), from French and English papermaking, challenged the model: paperworkers 'already labored exhausting hours at the outset of de Vries's period of newfound industriousness', and women and adolescents worked for wages long before it (abstract). See economic/household_demand, consumption/household_labor and global/protoindustry_trade_limits for the field contributions.
strands.works: Mendels (JEH 1972) and NYRB letter (1984); Kriedte, Medick and Schlumbohm (1977; English 1981); Medick (1976); Coleman (1983); de Vries (1994; 2008); van Nederveen Meerkerk (2009); Rosenband (2016)

strands.title: Why Britain? Energy, knowledge and wages, 1988–2023
strands.focus: Wrigley (1988) questioned the Industrial Revolution as 'a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon' and contrasted an 'organic economy' bounded by land with a mineral-based energy regime. Mokyr's 'Industrial Enlightenment' was 'the key to sustained and accelerating invention' (2002 draft); reviewing The Enlightened Economy (2009), Harley questioned whether the Industrial Enlightenment explained economic change or largely redescribed it (2010). Allen (2009) argued that 'Wages were remarkably high, and energy was remarkably cheap', so 'it paid to invent it there'; Humphries charged the high-wage account with a 'patriarchal perspective' (2013), and Allen replied with evidence 'that women and children participated in the high wage economy' (2015, abstract). Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda found that, across English counties, industrialisation occurred where wages began low and mechanical skills high (2023); the result concerns differences within England, not Britain's international wage advantage. The article sets it 'directly counter' to Allen's argument (pp. 60–61), as their 2014 essay had argued from British workers' human capital against his high wages. Clark and Jacks's coal-rent estimates imply a negligible income contribution from England's possession of coal reserves (2007). See economic/wrigley_growth and technology/invention_adoption.
strands.works: Wrigley, Continuity, Chance and Change (1988), The Path to Sustained Growth (2016); Mokyr (2002 paper), The Enlightened Economy (2009); Harley (2010); Allen (2009; 2015); Humphries (2013); Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2014; 2023); Clark and Jacks (2007)

strands.title: The Great Divergence and the so-called California School, 1997–2021
strands.focus: Wong (1997) challenged Europe's status as the comparative norm. Pomeranz (2000) followed 'a procedure outlined in Wong's recent China Transformed' while giving 'greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures', and greater weight to ecological constraints, coal and New World resources; he dated divergence late. Readers attribute the label 'California School' to Goldstone (Frank 2001; Vries 2009), whose 'efflorescences' (2002) put pre-modern growth outside Europe too while locating the modern breakthrough in British engines, science and craft culture. Frank's ReOrient (1998) and a debate with Landes scheduled for December 1998, announced in a notice written from Frank's side, marked the polemical poles. Parthasarathi carried the argument to India (2011). Rosenthal and Wong explained divergence by political fragmentation and war (2011, as Ma's review reports and Wong restated in 2016); Ma found the hypothesis 'supported by fairly meager evidence'. Critics answered from property relations (Brenner and Isett 2002), knowledge (Mokyr 2002, 2012), wages and national accounts (Broadberry and Gupta 2006; Allen et al. 2011; Broadberry, Guan and Li 2021) and the state (Vries 2009, 2013). The Huang–Pomeranz exchange stays in economic/divergence_household_dispute and economic/coal_constraints_dispute.

strands.title: Capitalism and Slavery and its critics: the Williams thesis, 1944–2020
strands.focus: Williams (1944) advanced distinct propositions, which readers keep apart: that slave-trade and plantation wealth financed and stimulated British industry; that slave-derived wealth mattered in eighteenth-century Britain; and that the West Indies' economic decline, with changing economic interests, explains abolition. Drescher's Econocide (1977), in its publisher's description, challenged decline-based explanations of the 1807 abolition and stressed public mobilisation; Solow and Engerman's volume (1987) sifted the 'legacy'. Solow judged that slavery 'did not cause the Industrial Revolution but played an active role in its pattern and timing' (as quoted by Burnard and Riello), while Eltis and Engerman (2000), as Hilt and Burnard and Riello report them, judged its growth linkages to British industry small. Inikori (2002), as O'Rourke reports, reasserted the thesis through Atlantic trade and African producers and consumers. Hall (2014) and Burnard and Riello (2020) identify modified Williams arguments in Pomeranz and Inikori. The Legacies of British Slave-ownership team investigates slave-ownership's British legacies; its compensation evidence supports some Williams propositions, on slave-derived wealth, and qualifies the decline thesis, while leaving the industrialisation controversy unresolved ('Our material cannot resolve these controversies'). See economic/empire and atlantic/earlier.
strands.works: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery (1944); Drescher, Econocide (1977) and 'Capitalism and Slavery after Fifty Years' (1997); Solow and Engerman (eds), British Capitalism and Caribbean Slavery (1987); Eltis and Engerman (JEH 2000); Inikori, Africans and the Industrial Revolution in England (2002); Hall et al., Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014)

strands.title: Slavery's capitalism and its economic-historian critics, 2013–2020
strands.focus: This strand selects the slavery controversy within the broader history of capitalism, a field whose early definition by Beckert, Hilt notes, is so broad that it 'includes most of the fields of labor, political, social, and business history', and whose work, Regele notes, began before the 2007–2009 financial crisis. Mainly Americanist historians, publicised as historians of capitalism in 2013, put slavery at the centre of American and global capitalism: Johnson's River of Dark Dreams (2013; Johnson does not count himself a historian of capitalism, Hilt notes), Baptist's argument, in Hilt's account, that torture drove cotton productivity (2014), Beckert's 'war capitalism' (2014) and Beckert and Rockman's Slavery's Capitalism (2016). Olmstead and Rhode answered that the books 'make fundamental errors in economic reasoning' (2017); Hilt, that 'specious arguments and failures of analytical reasoning sometimes undermine' them as social criticism, while granting that economic research supports some of their arguments and calling for 'dialogue, if not collaboration' (2017); Burnard and Riello, that US cotton came 'too late to cause an Industrial Revolution' (2020). Readers trace the movement to Polanyi, the 2008 crisis and a turn from labour history (Hilt; Regele) and to Williams and Pomeranz (Burnard and Riello). Fogel and Engerman's earlier slavery debate stays in quant/slavery_debate.
